Afrinext · authentication · email, password and the programme choice

Chosen Is Not Paid

Email and password are now the main way in, phone sign-in keeps working for every account that already exists, and signup asks which programme somebody wants before it asks for anything else. The hard part was not the forms. It was keeping four things apart that one column would have merged: the programme chosen, the subscription's state, the payment, and what somebody is entitled to right now. No payment provider exists, so nothing can be entitled to anything — and the code makes that structurally true rather than merely currently true.

Branch claude/create-app-repository-1cxsih Code at 7feadac Unit tests 736 passed, 20 skipped Browser tests 54 passed Mutations 19 / 19 caught Ledger touched none Email provider still none
Read this first: three things this milestone does not do

No email is delivered anywhere. No provider is chosen, so ConsoleSender is what runs and it writes what it would have sent to the log. Verification and reset codes are exercised end to end in development, CI and preview by reading that log. They reach no inbox. Section H says exactly what remains.

No Entrepreneur subscription can become active. Choosing the paid programme writes a pending_payment row that grants nothing. There is deliberately no activate() function anywhere: with no payment provider implemented, anything able to set active today would set it because a button was pressed.

No existing account was migrated, backfilled or deleted. Migration 0016 is additive only. Phone accounts keep their invented @phone.afrinext.local address exactly as it is, keep their sessions, their roles, their wallet and their ledger history. Section E is the evidence.

A

The four things kept apart

Your constraint was precise: "choisir Entrepreneur ne veut jamais dire que l'abonnement est payé ou actif", and "ne crée pas une architecture qui empêcherait un utilisateur Vendeur de devenir Entrepreneur sans créer un deuxième compte". Both are structural, so both are enforced by where the data lives rather than by a rule somebody has to remember.

ThingWhere it livesWhat it means
Programme chosenusers.programmeA declared intent. Grants no role, unlocks no feature, and is never consulted by authorize().
Subscription stateprogramme_subscriptions.statuspending_payment → active → past_due / cancelled / expired. Today only the first is reachable.
Paymentorders / paymentsNot touched by this milestone at all. iPayMoney remains unimplemented.
EntitlementDerived, never storedisEntitled() — an active row whose period covers the clock. A cached entitlement is a bill somebody stopped paying that nobody noticed.

Why a column on users and not a row somewhere else

Because a person has exactly one current programme, and because moving between them has to be an UPDATE on the account they already have. Same users.id throughout — which is what their roles, their store, their wallet, their orders and every ledger entry ever posted against them are keyed on. There is no path in the code that asks anybody to open a second account, and the test suite asserts there is not: after an upgrade, select count(*) from users is still 1 and auth_user_id is unchanged.

Why there is no activate()

The absence is the feature

active is declared in the state machine and is unreachable from application code. Writing an activation function now would mean either taking a payment reference nothing can verify, or taking none at all — and the second is precisely how a subscription becomes active because a button was pressed.

A test asserts the absence rather than describing it: after choosing Entrepreneur, select count(*) from programme_subscriptions where status = 'active' is 0, and the browser journey additionally asserts no order, no payment and no ledger account was created. If a later change adds a way to activate without a verified payment, that test fails.

The price is data

2 000 FCFA is what the business decided today, not a constant of the software. It is a default in PROGRAMME_PRICES and an UPDATE in platform_settings under programme.pricing — the same posture as the OTP policy. Each field is validated on its own, so a malformed row cannot make the programme free or land it in the wrong currency; anything unusable falls back to the reviewed default rather than through it.

XOF has zero decimal places, so 2 000 francs is 2000n minor units. Writing 200000n — the reflex from two-decimal currencies — would charge a hundred times the price and nothing downstream would catch it. That is mutation E16, and it is caught.

B

What was built

Migration 0016 — additive only

-- one CHECK widened, one column added, one table created. Nothing rewritten.
ALTER TABLE otp_challenges DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS otp_purpose_valid;
ALTER TABLE otp_challenges ADD CONSTRAINT otp_purpose_valid CHECK (purpose IN
  ('sign_in','verify_identity','step_up','email_verification','password_reset'));

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS programme TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'vendeur';

CREATE TABLE programme_subscriptions (... status, price_minor, currency, period ...);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX programme_subscriptions_one_live ON programme_subscriptions
  (user_id, programme) WHERE status IN ('pending_payment','active','past_due');

Four rules are enforced by PostgreSQL rather than by application code, because the application is not the only thing that will ever write to these tables:

ConstraintRefuses
programme_subscriptions_one_liveA second live subscription for one person. Two pending_payment rows is two invoices for one month, and whichever the provider confirms leaves the other looking unpaid for ever. Cancelled and expired rows are excluded, so history is never overwritten.
…_active_has_periodAn active subscription with no billing period.
…_price_positiveA free or negative price on a paid programme.
users_programme_validA programme the application does not know.

Referral and the activation bonus, precisely

No referral model was invented and no referral code was written. Searching the repository for the word does return hits, and honesty is better than a clean-sounding claim: they are all pre-existing, from Phase 0 and Phase 1, and none is logic. A referral_terms value in the legal-document kind CHECK, a referral value in the fee-line key column, and two comments in ledger and money/allocate explaining why a commission basis is not always the gross.

For the activation bonus the claim is absolute and was verified the same way: there is no constant, no column, no table, no transaction, no state and no code path named for it or implementing it — no REFERRAL_ACTIVATION, no 1 000 FCFA anywhere. Nothing was removed either, because nothing was ever there.

The programme endpoint says what it means

{ "data": { "programme": "entrepreneur",
             "subscriptionStatus": "pending_payment",
             // named `entitled`, never `active`, and never derived from the choice
             "entitled": false,
             "priceMinor": "2000", "currency": "XOF" } }

Minor units go out as a string with the currency alongside, because JSON.stringify throws on a bigint — a useful accident that forces every transport to say how an amount is represented rather than letting one quietly become a float.

C

Codes, and what they cannot leak

Email verification and password reset use the authoritative challenge mechanism, not a second one. Same table, same keyed HMAC, same database-enforced properties. Two values were added to the purpose CHECK and nothing else changed.

PropertyEnforced by
The code exists in exactly one place, as a hashotp_challenges.code_hash, HMAC-SHA256 under a key derived from the application secret. A plain digest of a six-digit code is reversible by trying all million inputs; the key is what a stolen table does not contain.
One live challenge per identifier and purposePartial unique index. Banking several usable codes and spending each one's attempt budget is not possible.
Bounded attemptswhere attempts < max_attempts — a predicate, not a number this process is trusted to remember.
Single usewhere consumed_at is null.
Verification and reset cannot be swappedThe purpose is in the hash and in the lookup. A verification code presented to the reset endpoint is refused, and the reverse. Mutation E7.

No leak about whether an address exists

You asked for this explicitly. It holds in three places at once, and the third is the one that is usually forgotten:

  1. The body and the status are identical. An address with an account, one without, and a phone account's unreachable synthetic address all answer { "sent": true }.
  2. Every verification failure is identical. Wrong code, expired code, no challenge at all, exhausted attempts, synthetic address — one 400 auth.otp_invalid. The real reason goes to the log.
  3. The rate limit is consumed BEFORE the address is judged. Limiting only real, reachable addresses would make the limiter itself the oracle: an attacker learns which addresses exist by seeing which ones eventually answer 429 and which ones never do. Every request costs a token, including the ones that lead nowhere. Mutation E11.
Tested, not asserted

The browser test drives the real form twice — once with an address that has an account, once with one that does not — and compares the rendered text of the notice and the step the form advances to. Same words, same next screen. A form that only advanced for real addresses would leak exactly what the message refuses to.

Issuance is limited, and the limits are configuration

Bounding attempts alone protects nothing if fresh codes can be requested without limit. The first draft of this carried limit: 5 inline — which is the defect review decision 7 already ruled on for SMS — so the rules moved into ratelimit as emailSendRules(), reading a new perEmailPerHour field on the stored policy. Changing a limit stays an UPDATE, not a deploy.

It is a separate field from perPhonePerHour because the two cost different things: an SMS is money out of the door on every send, an email spends the sending domain's reputation, and a mailbox that receives forty Afrinext codes in an hour marks the next one as spam for everybody.

The synthetic address, and why it gets its own helper

Phone signup mints <digits>@phone.afrinext.local to satisfy Better Auth's NOT NULL UNIQUE email column. That address is a placeholder wearing the costume of a real one: valid to the schema, unique, and it will never receive mail. The TLD does not resolve, and anybody may stand up a host that answers for it.

One helper, three call sites — sign-in refuses one, reset never sends to one, the banner offers "add an email" rather than "verify" one. Spelling the check inline in three places is how the fourth place forgets.

D

Reset, logout, sessions

A reset ends every session, and that is the point of it

Not housekeeping afterwards. A reset that leaves an attacker's session alive has achieved nothing: the person whose account it is changes their password, feels safe, and the intruder is still signed in on another device. Better Auth's session table is the only session store there is, so deleting the rows is signing those devices out — one statement, inside the same transaction as the password write.

The current session goes too. The screen then sends the person to sign in with the password they just chose, which is the honest ending: a reset means every existing session is suspect, including this one.

Proved in a browser, with two of them

The test signs the same account in on a second browser context, resets the password from the first, and then asserts that the second one's /api/v1/me answers 401 and that select count(*) from session for that account is 0. The old password is then refused and the new one works. Mutation E8 deletes the revocation; it is caught.

Logout

Sign-out is in the Menu drawer and goes through Better Auth, which deletes the session row. The token is dead for anybody holding it the moment it returns, not merely missing from this browser — a client that only cleared its own cookie would leave a live row behind. The browser test asserts the row count, then that /api/v1/me answers 401, then that /fr/wallet redirects to sign-in.

A second test asserts the opposite for the other devices: signing out on one does not sign out the others. Signing out is not a security event on the account; a reset is. That line is easy to blur in the wrong direction.

Better Auth writes the credential, and Afrinext writes it back

The reset writes account.password directly, which is the one place this milestone reaches into Better Auth's tables. It is safe because Better Auth is configured with Afrinext's own scrypt on both sides — but that is a configuration fact, and a configuration fact deserves a test. So one drives the real Better Auth instance: reset the password through the domain, then sign in through signInEmail with the new one and fail with the old.

The update is scoped to providerId = 'credential', because an account can hold one row per provider. Unscoped, the write puts a password hash into a field an OAuth provider owns, and on an account with several rows it becomes luck rather than logic which one Better Auth then verifies against. Mutation E10 removes the scope — and survived the first matrix, because every account in the suite had exactly one row for it to be wrong about. Section G.

Accounts that existed before this milestone

Your instruction was to preserve them without a mass backfill and without turning their invented addresses into real ones. Nothing migrates them. The evidence is a test group of its own, driving the real phone flow:

ClaimHow it is proved
Phone sign-in still worksThe whole existing browser suite signs in by phone — 46 tests, all passing. The screen now opens on email, so each taps through to the phone flow first.
The synthetic address is untouchedAsserted to still end in @phone.afrinext.local and to be unreachable. Not rewritten, not deleted.
Existing sessions surviveSession count is asserted before and after. Nothing in this change revokes them — revoking every existing seller's session for a schema addition would be an outage dressed as caution.
Roles and permissions holdAsserted across a programme change in both directions.
The programme default is the migration's, not a backfillvendeur, with no subscription row at all.
They can take the paid programme without a second accountSame users.id, same auth_user_id, same session, one row in users.
They cannot be taken over through the reset flowThe interesting attack, below.
The attack the quarantine exists to stop

A phone account has an address in user.email. A reset flow that merely looked the address up would send a code to <digits>@phone.afrinext.local — a domain that does not exist, which anybody could register and stand up a mail server for. Whoever did that would then hold a password-reset code for a real seller's account, with its store, its wallet and its ledger balance.

Two layers stop it: nothing issues a code to such an address, and nothing accepts one. The second layer is what my first test failed to check — see section G.

Nothing was removed

Per your instruction not to remove the old mechanism until compatibility is assured: the phone OTP flow is unchanged. Not deprecated, not hidden, not behind a flag. It is one tap from the sign-in screen and labelled as a choice rather than as a fallback, because for those accounts it is not an alternative — it is the only way in, and they have no password at all.

If you re-run these

The suite truncates the tables it touches, so two vitest runs against the same TEST_DATABASE_URL at once deadlock each other and fail in ledger/concurrency, content/storage-equivalence and payments/ipaymoney-replay — modules with nothing to do with this work. I did that to myself once and spent a few minutes believing I had broken the ledger. Run one at a time. Similarly, pnpm test:e2e serves whatever .next already holds, so a source change needs pnpm build first; CI does that as its own step.

Mutation matrix

All 19 mutations are caught. Every one fails at least one test, so each guarantee in this document is checked by something that would break if the guarantee were removed — rather than merely described in prose.

Each mutation is applied to the source in a detached worktree with its own database, the whole core suite is run, and the file is restored. Not a subset: narrowing the suite is how a mutation survives for the wrong reason, which the Phase 5 matrix learned the hard way.

Three defects that were in the code before the tests found them

1 · Signup never signed anybody in

emailAndPassword.autoSignIn is false, deliberately — consent has not been given at that point, so a session issued by signup would be a session for an account that resolves to no actor. My flow assumed a session existed after signUp.email and called the programme endpoint next. That call would have answered 401, and so would the consent fetch after it. The screen now signs in explicitly. Found by writing the integration test against the real Better Auth instance instead of against my reading of its configuration.

2 · A duplicate address returns success

signUpEmail on an address that already exists returns a success shape — a user object with token: null — and creates nothing. A caller reading "no error" as "account created" sails straight past it. The screen now tells the two apart the only way available from outside: it tries the credentials, and reports the address as taken when they do not work. A signup form saying an address is taken IS an enumeration surface, and an unavoidable one — a form that silently accepted a duplicate would be broken instead. The endpoints that do have a choice, reset and verification, are the ones that answer identically.

3 · APP_URL decides whether email sign-in works at all

It becomes Better Auth's baseURL, and Better Auth refuses any request whose Origin does not match it — INVALID_ORIGIN, before the handler runs. The browser servers answered on 127.0.0.1:31xx while claiming to be localhost:3000, so every signup and every email sign-in was rejected.

The same misconfiguration in production refuses every email sign-in while the phone flow keeps working, because the phone flow goes through Afrinext's own plugin endpoints and never meets that check — which is exactly what makes the breakage look partial and impossible to diagnose. render.yaml already declared APP_URL as sync: false; its comment said a wrong value meant "links point at localhost". It now says what it actually costs. This is item 1 in section H.

And three weak tests of my own

The matrix is worth running because it grades the tests, not the code. Three of mine were passing for the wrong reason, and the first two are the same mistake in two places.

E2 and E3 — an assertion satisfied by a later failure

Deleting the synthetic-address check from resetPassword broke nothing. With issuance already quarantined there is never a code to present, so the refusal came from "no challenge" either way — my assertion was satisfied by a later failure, which is no assertion at all. Same for confirmEmailVerification. That is the same defect the S8 finding named in the object-storage milestone, committed again by me in a new place.

The fix reaches the second layer on its own: the challenge is written one level below issueAndSend — the state a future code path or a hand-run migration could produce — and the reset is still refused with a valid code in hand. Same for verification, where accepting one would stamp emailVerified on a mailbox that cannot exist, and that flag is what every later account-recovery decision will lean on.

E10 — a scope with nothing to prove itself against

Removing providerId = 'credential' from the reset's password write broke no test, because every account in the suite had exactly one row in account. With one row the scope makes no observable difference, so nothing was checking it. The new test gives the account a second provider row: unscoped, the write puts a password hash into a field an OAuth provider owns, and on an account with several rows it becomes luck rather than logic which one Better Auth then verifies against.

Two defects the screenshots found, that no test would have

  • A signed-in person visiting /sign-in met a sign-in form with the unverified banner above it — two contradictions in one screen. Now redirected, on currentActor() rather than on a session, because a pending_consent account holds a session and still needs that page to render its consent step.
  • The banner rendered on the verification screen itself, so its action linked to the page you were already reading and its "Plus tard" sat directly above a second "Plus tard" meaning something else.
H

What remains before production

In the order it blocks things.

  1. Set APP_URL in Render, correctly, before anyone tries to sign in.

    The service's own public HTTPS URL. It is sync: false, so Render asks for it rather than assuming — and it is not knowable until Render has created the service. Until it is right, every email sign-in and every signup is refused while phone sign-in keeps working, which is the most confusing possible failure. No code change can fix this from here; it is a value only you can supply.

  2. Choose an email provider, and I will write the adapter.

    Nothing is configured and this milestone does not pretend otherwise. MessageSender is already the whole surface — no provider SDK reaches the domain, exactly as PaymentProvider and ContentStorage are handled — so an adapter is the only new code. I did not invent a provider or an API.

    Worth comparing on deliverability to African inboxes and on price: Resend, Postmark, Brevo, Amazon SES. Once chosen, the variables follow the CONTENT_S3_* posture — EMAIL_PROVIDER, EMAIL_API_KEY (secret, sync: false), EMAIL_FROM, EMAIL_REPLY_TO — declared in render.yaml, never valued in Git.

    Until then: ConsoleSender runs, refuses NODE_ENV=production without ALLOW_CONSOLE_SENDER=yes, and codes are read from the log. Acceptable for a preview. Never for production.

  3. Decide what the Entrepreneur subscription costs and how it is paid.

    The price is already data — an UPDATE on platform_settings, not a deploy. The payment is not: it needs iPayMoney, whose adapter still throws rather than pretending, and whose documentation is still unavailable. Until then a subscription can only be pending_payment and the screens say so in plain French.

    When the provider exists, activation is one function and one test: a subscription becomes active only against a verified payment, with a period, and the guard test in section A is what will tell you if a later change smuggled in a second route.

  4. Decide what happens to a phone account that wants an address.

    Nothing backfills one, deliberately — that was your instruction and it is the right one. What does not exist yet is the screen where somebody chooses to add one: verify the new address, then swap it in place of the synthetic one. That is a small milestone of its own, and it is the thing that eventually lets the synthetic domain be retired.

  5. Deploy and re-run the browser suite against the deployment.

    Everything here ran against a local production build. The preview deployment is still blocked on the same thing the R2 milestone was: this sandbox cannot reach onrender.com.

Nothing here needs a decision from me

Items 1 and 5 are values and access only you have. Item 2 is a commercial choice. Item 3 waits on iPayMoney. Item 4 is the next milestone whenever you want it. The code is complete for what this milestone was asked to do, and honestly described as: email and password work, no email is delivered, and no subscription can be paid for.
